transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you. Well, what brings me in is... I realized recently that I keep arranging my own house around not seeing spiders. 

I mean, I put off doing the laundry for days just because the machine is down in the basement. I completely avoid the garden shed. I've even started paying people to do small maintenance jobs around the house that I know perfectly well how to do myself, simply because I can’t make myself go into those spaces. It's just getting to be too much of a disruption to my life.
When you're in a situation where you can't avoid spiders—say, you unexpectedly encounter one—do you find yourself having repetitive, unwanted thoughts about it that are hard to get out of your head?

No, not really. I don't... I don't get stuck thinking about them all day, if that's what you mean. It's more about the immediate moment. If I see one, I just panic and have to get away from it right then and there. But once I know it's gone or I'm safely out of the room, I don't keep having thoughts about it playing on a loop in my head. I just absolutely do not want to be near them in the first place.

When you know you might encounter a spider—like before going into the basement or garden shed—do you start feeling anxious, nervous, or physical symptoms like a racing heart or sweating before you even see one?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I don't stand at the top of the basement stairs sweating or with my heart pounding, if that's what you mean. 

It's more that I just... I just make a firm decision not to go down there. I know there's a good chance I'll see one, so I just avoid the space entirely to be safe. The actual panic, the racing heart and all that... that really only happens if one is actually right in front of me.

When you're about to go into the basement or shed, and you're thinking about the possibility of seeing a spider there, do you notice any anxiety or nervousness building up as you approach the door—even before you actually go in?

Well, like I was saying, I don't really get nervous beforehand. I mean, I don't walk up to the basement door and start feeling anxious or anything. I just... I just decide not to go. If I think about there being a spider, I just skip doing whatever it was I needed to do down there. It's not a buildup of anxiety, it's just avoiding it altogether so I don't have to deal with it.

Let me ask this differently: when you're actually walking toward the basement door—not before, but in that moment—do you feel any dread, fear, or discomfort building up, or is it purely a rational decision with no emotional reaction until you might actually see a spider?

No, there's no dread or fear building up as I walk toward the door. It's just a practical decision for me. I know there might be a spider, so I just stop and decide not to go in. I don't feel any discomfort or emotional reaction until there's actually a spider right in front of me.

I want to make sure I understand this correctly: if you were standing right at the basement door with your hand on the knob, about to open it, would you feel any fear, anxiety, or physical discomfort in that moment, or would it truly feel like just a calm, rational decision to turn around?

Honestly, if I were standing right there with my hand on the knob... I still don't think I'd feel that rush of fear or anything. It really is just a calm decision. I just think, "No, there's probably a spider down there," and I turn around. The panic just doesn't hit me unless I actually see one.

If you absolutely had to go into the basement for an important reason—say, to retrieve something critical—and you knew you might see a spider, would you feel fear or anxiety building up as you prepared to go down, or would it still feel like just a logical decision with no emotional component?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. If it was something truly critical... well, I usually just find a workaround. I'll ask my husband to get it, or I just wait until someone else is around. 

I haven't actually been in a situation where I was completely forced to go down there alone with no other option. So... I don't really know if the fear would build up beforehand in that specific case. I just know that, normally, I avoid it entirely so I don't have to find out.

Let me ask you this: suppose your husband wasn't home and the basement flooded—you absolutely had to go down there right then to turn off the water. In that moment, as you're about to go down those stairs knowing a spider might be there, would you feel your heart racing, sweating, or intense fear building up as you approach, or would it still feel calm and rational?

Well... if it was an emergency like a flood, I suppose I would have to go down there. But honestly, I just don't let it get to that point. I arrange my whole life around not having to go into those spaces. 

Like, I put off doing laundry because the machine is in the basement. I completely avoid the garden shed. I even pay handymen to do small repairs that I know perfectly well how to do myself, just because I can't make myself go into those areas where a spider might be. I just organize my house and my routine so I never have to endure that situation in the first place.
